articles.title: The Foil Podcast breaks down light-wind SailGP practice racing in Rio

hero.alt: SailGP practice racing in Rio de Janeiro

articles.byline: The Foil Podcast  ·  SailGP Rio de Janeiro
articles.placement1_label: Fan Reactions · Rio de Janeiro · Powered by Genuin
articles.body_intro:
Reporting from Rio de Janeiro, Bene and Andy delivered an on-the-ground recap of a tricky SailGP practice day marked by rain, very light breeze, and what they described as marginal foiling conditions. The pair said they spent several hours watching practice races that may ultimately prove more valuable for reading relative team form than for predicting the weekend outright, given how different Rio can look when the wind fills in.

The practice session was split into two racing groups, a six-boat group and a seven-boat group. Bene and Andy noted that those groups could be merged into a single fleet for the main racing, which would change the tactical picture significantly. Even so, they came away struck by how familiar the top of the results sheet looked: Australia and Spain each collected two practice wins, with Sweden and Great Britain taking one apiece. In their view, that clustering reinforced a sense that the usual contenders are again setting the pace at the start of the season, with New Zealand also considered among the favorites even if the practice results were not the focus of this particular recap.

One of the standout teams in the light air, they said, was Spain. Andy pointed to the Spanish crew, referred to as "Los Gallos," as looking notably in control in the marginal conditions, particularly in their ability to keep the boat foiling or close to foiling when others struggled. Bene argued that kind of efficiency in borderline wind is often a separator in SailGP, where small differences in takeoff and stability can turn into big gains on the racecourse.

France, by contrast, sounded like a team still bedding in changes. Bene and Andy said they expected more from a squad that is typically among the front runners, but suggested the day's uneven performance could be linked to new personnel on board following a crash in Auckland. They highlighted that even after winning a start, France slipped back to fifth relatively quickly in one race, which they took as a sign that the team's current setup and coordination may not be fully dialed in yet. In their telling, the reshuffle included Andy Ashby in a wing-trim role, and a strategy change that replaced Manon Éon with Liv Mackay.

Away from the racing itself, the pair also shared a brief dockside conversation with Brazilian sailing icon Robert Scheidt, describing him as a multi-time Olympic medalist who was in Rio watching the training. According to Bene and Andy, Scheidt's message was optimistic: he had seen strong conditions in training the day before and felt Rio rarely delivers multiple poor wind days in a row. That left them hoping Friday's light-air practice would be the outlier, with better breeze arriving for Saturday and, especially, Sunday.

Ultimately, Bene and Andy framed the practice session as a difficult watch for fans of high-speed foiling, but not a reason to downshift expectations for the weekend. With crowds expected to increase and the forecast trending toward stronger wind later in the event window, they suggested the stage was set for Rio to still deliver the kind of fast, dramatic SailGP racing the circuit is known for.

For more from the show, see The Foil Podcast.
articles.body_mid:
What to watch this weekend

With stronger breeze forecast for Saturday and Sunday, the teams that struggled in the marginal light-air conditions could look very different in a proper Rio sea breeze. Spain's light-wind efficiency is impressive, but the real test will be whether "Los Gallos" can carry that composure into the high-speed foiling conditions that define SailGP at its best.

France's reshuffle remains the biggest question mark heading into race day — whether the new crew combinations can gel quickly enough to challenge the established frontrunners, or whether the changes represent a longer-term rebuild that will take time to pay off.
articles.body_outro:
The takeaway

A difficult practice day doesn't define what Rio will deliver. Robert Scheidt's optimism, backed by local knowledge of a venue that rarely produces consecutive poor wind days, gives Bene and Andy — and the fans — reason to believe the weekend still has plenty of fast, dramatic SailGP racing in store.

articles.title: Outteridge on home water: "We've been waiting three years for this weekend."

hero.alt: Nathan Outteridge portrait on the dock

articles.byline: By R. Kawhena  ·  9 min read  ·  SailGP Auckland
articles.body_intro:
Nathan Outteridge has sailed in four Olympic Games, won a silver medal in London and a gold in Rio, and competed at the highest level of match racing for over a decade. But sitting across from him in the Japan SailGP Team briefing room at the Viaduct, 48 hours before the Auckland Grand Prix, there's something different about him. He's home — and it shows.

"Auckland is where it started for me," he says, leaning forward slightly. "Every sailor from this part of the world dreams about racing here. It's the water we grew up on. The Waitemata — I know every shift, every pressure line on this harbour. It matters."

Three years in the making

The Japan team hasn't raced in Auckland since the 2021-22 season. Two schedule changes and a venue rotation kept them away. For Outteridge — born in Sydney but long based in Auckland — the wait has been personal as much as professional.

Q — You said you've been waiting three years. What does that actually mean for your preparation?
"It means we've banked a lot. I've been out here on my own, on a Laser, just getting re-acquainted with the pressure. The way the breeze builds off the Waitakere Ranges in the afternoon — that's local knowledge you can't get from a model. We've been building this race plan for months."

The Japan project

Japan SailGP sits fourth in the championship standings, a position that doesn't fully reflect how competitive they've become over the past 18 months. The team's boat speed in light-to-medium conditions has improved markedly — partly through technical developments, partly through the grinding physical conditioning of the crew.

"A year ago we were fifth or sixth in boat speed at 12 knots. Now I genuinely believe we're third. That's not an accident — the team has done brutal work." — Nathan Outteridge

He won't be drawn on specifics — the team's technical programme is kept closely guarded — but the data from the practice sessions at the Viaduct supports his assessment. Japan was fastest through the bottom gate in four of the six practice runs, consistently generating 51+ knots in a 16-knot south-westerly.

What Auckland means for the title race

With five events remaining after Auckland, Japan needs results. A win or second in either of this weekend's races keeps their championship bid mathematically alive. Outteridge is characteristically direct about the stakes: "We're not here for top five. We're here to win."
articles.body_mid:
Life at the top

Away from the racing, Outteridge is thoughtful about what a second chapter at the elite level looks like. He's 37 — young by any conventional measure, but deep in sailing years — and has no immediate plans to slow down. "This circuit is the most physically and tactically demanding thing I've done," he says. "Honestly, more than the Olympics. Because you're doing it every two weeks, at full intensity, against the same people who are also improving every race."

Q — Is there life after SailGP?
"Ask me in three years. Right now I just want to win the Auckland Grand Prix. That's the whole conversation."

He stands, the briefing over, and moves toward the harbour-side windows. Out on the Waitemata, two F50s are doing speed runs in the afternoon breeze, spray arcing off their bows. He watches for a moment without speaking. Then: "Yeah. This is the one."

articles.title: Why wing trim is where the Aussies are losing half a knot.

hero.alt: F50 wing sail detail in carbon fibre

articles.byline: By M. Cole  ·  8 min read  ·  Performance Analysis
articles.body_intro:
Half a knot doesn't sound like much. In SailGP, it's the difference between first and fourth. And over the last three events, Australia's telemetry has revealed a consistent pattern: they are losing between 0.4 and 0.6 knots of boat speed in the 18–24 knot wind range, specifically during upwind legs — and the data points to wing trim as the primary cause.

This isn't speculation. The SailGP performance data package — available to credentialled analysts through the league's data platform — shows Australia consistently carrying a flatter wing chord angle than their top rivals in the upper wind range. The result is a boat that points higher but moves slower. It's a trim philosophy that worked brilliantly in lighter conditions but is costing them dearly as the season moves into breezier venues.

Understanding the wing geometry

The F50's rigid wing sail operates on principles closer to an aircraft wing than a traditional sail. Camber (curvature depth), twist (variation in angle from base to tip), and angle of attack all interact dynamically as wind speed changes. In moderate breeze — 12 to 17 knots — Australia's trim settings have been optimal. Their average upwind VMG in this range leads the fleet.

TeamAvg Upwind VMG (12–17 kn)Avg Upwind VMG (18–24 kn)Delta
Denmark18.2 kn19.8 kn+1.6
Great Britain17.9 kn19.4 kn+1.5
Japan17.7 kn19.1 kn+1.4
Australia18.4 kn19.1 kn+0.7
New Zealand17.5 kn18.8 kn+1.3

Australia leads in the lighter range — their 18.4 knot average is best in fleet. But when the breeze climbs above 18 knots, their improvement is less than half the fleet average. They are leaving 0.7–0.9 knots on the table compared to Denmark and Great Britain in breeze.

"The wing is a compromise every time you set it. You trim for the puff you're in, and three seconds later the puff is gone. The question is which compromise costs you least over a full race." — Technical analyst, anonymous

Where the half-knot goes

The core issue appears to be Australia's chord depth setting in the upper-wing panels. Compared to Denmark — who lead the fleet in high-wind VMG — Australia are running approximately 4–6% less camber in the top third of the wing. This flattens the sail and reduces drag, which is correct logic at 25+ knots. But at 18–22 knots, it's over-correcting, starving the wing of drive at precisely the moment the boat needs to accelerate through the power band.
articles.body_mid:
Can they fix it?

The short answer is yes — but it requires trust. Changing trim philosophy mid-season is uncomfortable. The settings Australia have been using in the 18–24 knot range feel correct to the wing trimmer because they've been reinforced by success in lighter conditions. Breaking that feedback loop takes deliberate data-led decision-making, and the pressure of championship racing doesn't always create the right environment for that.

The upcoming Plymouth event typically produces consistent 18–22 knot sea-breeze conditions. If Australia arrive with the same trim package and the breeze fills in as forecast, they'll be staring at another half-knot deficit against the fleet leaders — at a venue where positions aren't easily recovered by aggressive tactics.

The bigger picture

What makes this analysis fascinating is that it reveals a truth about elite sport that applies far beyond sailing: often the gap isn't physical or strategic, it's technical — a small, precise choice made thousands of times over a race weekend, each one adding or subtracting fractions of boat speed. Australia's answer may be as simple as adding camber. But implementing that change under race pressure, with a championship on the line, is anything but simple.

articles.title: Inside the grinder's race: seven minutes of flat-out sprint.

hero.alt: F50 crew on the trampoline at speed, spray flying

articles.byline: By L. Dubois  ·  7 min read  ·  SailGP Auckland
articles.body_intro:
From the grandstand, Race 3 at the Auckland SailGP looked like a procession. Denmark led from the gun, crossed every gate first, and took the win by a comfortable margin. But the race within the race — the brutal, invisible contest happening on every F50's trampoline — was anything but comfortable. For seven minutes in the middle of the final reaching leg, the crew physicality demands hit levels that rival the most intense moments in professional sport.

We had access to France SailGP Team's crew data for this piece. What follows is a minute-by-minute account of what their bodies went through during that sequence.

The sequence, minute by minute

0:00 — Gate 3 exit
France rounds the leeward gate in fourth. Denmark is 180m clear. The tactical call is made: push for a bear-away at the layline, accelerate through the gust pocket tracking on the right. All four crew move to weather trampoline within 3 seconds.
1:20 — Acceleration phase
Boat speed climbs from 38.1 to 47.6 knots in 80 seconds. The grinders are cycling at maximum output — estimated 800+ watts per person. Heart rates spike above 170 bpm across the crew.
2:45 — Gust hit
A 4-knot puff arrives. The wing trimmer makes three rapid adjustments in 11 seconds. The boat leaps to 51.2 knots. Crew weight shifts 40cm aft to keep the bow up. One crew member momentarily loses footing — recovers without incident.
4:10 — Decision window
France has closed on Japan but faces a crossing situation with New Zealand coming from starboard. Helm calls the cross — 1.4m clearance. The grinders haven't stopped cycling. Average heart rate across crew: 181 bpm.
6:00 — Peak output
Approaching the top mark layline, France hits 53.4 knots — their fastest of the weekend. One crew member's heart rate peaks at 186 bpm. The boat is covering 27 metres per second. The crew are performing precision balance movements at that speed.
7:12 — Mark rounding
France rounds cleanly in third — one position gained, one lost during the gate. The seven-minute sprint ends. Average heart rates begin dropping from 182 bpm. Recovery window: approximately 40 seconds before the next acceleration demand.

"People think it's about the helmsman. It's about the four people on that trampoline who never stop moving, never stop producing power. They're the engine." — France SailGP Team, crew debrief
articles.body_mid:
What this tells us about SailGP athleticism

The seven-minute sequence France experienced is not unusual — it's race-normal for SailGP. What's unusual is having the data to see it clearly. Peak heart rates above 180 bpm sustained for extended periods, combined with balance demands that require constant micro-adjustments at 50+ knots, place SailGP crew among the most physically stressed athletes in any sport during racing.

For context: elite Tour de France cyclists sustain around 170–180 bpm on major climbs. Rugby players rarely exceed 185 bpm for more than brief sprints. SailGP crew are doing this while making split-second decisions at 53 knots, inches above the water, in full team coordination.

Why Denmark keeps winning

The Danish crew's fitness data — extrapolated from observable recovery patterns and post-race interviews — suggests they have developed an efficiency advantage: they reach the same boat speed output at lower peak heart rates than competitors. That means they have more physiological headroom in the decisive moments of a race. When every other crew is at 186 bpm and barely functional, Denmark's crew are at 174 and still making clean decisions.

That gap is the hardest thing in sport to close: not strength, not speed, but efficiency under extreme pressure. It's what separates the team at the top of the SailGP leaderboard from everyone chasing them.
